title: The booksellers' street
hookLine: Baghdad's book market, copyists and public libraries

lines: A SHEET, A PEN, A POT OF INK.
ONE CAREFUL HAND AT A TIME.
cards: A sheet of paper, a reed pen, a pot of ink. Now line a street with them.
Shop after shop, and in each one a person bent over a page, copying a book letter by letter, while customers wander in to browse, haggle, argue about poetry, or sit down and read.

In Abbasid Baghdad, the people who ran these shops had a name, warraq, and their market was known as the market of the warraqs. Before the printing press, this was how a book multiplied: one careful hand at a time.

teach.b: Warraq is built on waraq, a leaf, a sheet of paper. So a warraq is a paper person: a copyist, a stationer, a bookseller, often all three. Some were hired hands.
Some were scholars themselves, who copied books they loved and sold copies to pay the rent.
One bookseller's son in Baghdad did something remarkable with the trade: Ibn al-Nadim, whose catalogue named the astrolabe maker al-Ijliya three days ago.
He wrote the Fihrist, the Catalogue: a list of books and their authors, across grammar, poetry, law, the Qur'an's sciences, philosophy, medicine, even the beliefs of other peoples.
It reads like a walk down the shelves of his world, and it preserves the names of books that are now lost. Why did people care so much about pages?

By the usual account, the first words revealed to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, begin with a command to read, and go on, in Pickthall's translation: "Who teacheth by the pen, Teacheth man that which he knew not."
The pen sits right there in the opening of the revelation.

Around the shops there were libraries: collections in mosques, in schools, in the homes of patrons who opened their doors to readers. A student without money for a copy could still find a book to sit with.
So walk the street again. Ink on fingers. Paper stacked in bundles.
Someone reading aloud from a new copy to hear if it sounds right. A city where a book was a thing you could walk to.

how: Muslims honor the pen and the written word, and some mosques, schools and Islamic centers today keep libraries open to readers, continuing an old tradition of shared books.

games.q: you run a shop on the booksellers' street. a student wants his own copy of a book you have on the shelf. how does he get it?
o: you print a fresh copy for him.
a copyist writes it out by hand, page by page.
you lend him the only copy, forever.
games.why: there was no printing press. every new copy was written out by hand, which is why the copyists' street was the heart of the book trade.

practice: If there's a book within reach, pick it up and feel its weight and the edges of its pages; if not, bring to mind a library you know.
Think of the hands that made the book possible: the writer, whoever copied or printed it, whoever carried it to the shelf.
If you pray, you can let this minute be thanks for the pen; if not, let it be thanks for the people who kept the pages.

wordCard.voice: Warraq, a copyist, stationer and bookseller: the people who ran Baghdad's market of books, with libraries open to readers nearby. Today's word.
